title: A good thing to give thanks (Psalm 92:2)
hook: "It is a good thing to give thanks unto the LORD", the psalm of the Sabbath day

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lecha Dodi, and the room turning to the door. Your line was shake off the dust, arise. Who did you turn toward? Today, the psalm sung right after the bride arrives. Day six hundred sixteen.

Here's a small puzzle. There's a psalm the Mishnah calls the Sabbath's song. It says the Levites sang it in the Temple on Shabbat. Jews say it on Friday night and again on Saturday morning. Its title says, in so many words, for the Sabbath day. And then, in the whole psalm, the Sabbath is never mentioned again. Not once. No rest, no seventh day, no candles. So what makes it the Sabbath's song?
screen: `THE SABBATH PSALM.` → `SUNG BY THE LEVITES.` → `NEVER MENTIONS THE SABBATH.`

segments.voice: Psalm 92, in the old Jewish translation, opens with its title: "A Psalm, a Song. For the sabbath day." Then the first line: "It is a good thing to give thanks unto the LORD." And it goes on: to declare your lovingkindness in the morning, and your faithfulness in the night. Morning and night, the whole day, held in thanks. Then the psalm notices something hard. The wicked spring up like grass, it says. They seem to be winning. But grass is gone in a season. And the righteous? "The righteous shall flourish like the palm-tree." Like a cedar in Lebanon. Trees that grow slowly and stand a long time. So maybe that's the Sabbath in it. Six days you watch the grass: what's fast, loud, winning this week. On the seventh you look at the trees: what's slow, and lasting. The Mishnah offers another answer. It says this is a song for the time to come, for a day that will be entirely Sabbath. A world at rest. And a midrash tells a third story. Adam, it says, met his son Cain after the murder of Abel, and learned that Cain had repented and been given another chance. Adam was amazed and said: so great is the power of returning. And he sang this psalm. And some readers hear a second meaning in the opening line. The Hebrew for give thanks, l'hodot, shares its root with the word for confessing, admitting. It is good to give thanks. It is good to own up. After Adam's story, one word can carry both.
screen: `FOR THE SABBATH DAY.` · `MORNING AND NIGHT, IN THANKS.` · `GRASS, AND THE PALM TREE.` · `L'HODOT: THANK, AND CONFESS.` · then, large: `GOOD TO GIVE THANKS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give thanks for one good thing. Settle, and breathe. Look back at the week. Find one thing that was slow and good, a tree, not grass. A friendship that held. A habit you kept. A meal someone made. Name it. Say thank you for it, out loud or inside, to God if you pray, or to the person, or simply to the day. Then hold it, and let it be enough. The bell holds the time.
L'hodot. To give thanks: the first word of Psalm 92's opening line, the Sabbath psalm that never mentions the Sabbath.

Your line: good to give thanks. A week of Maariv, Hashkiveinu, the omer, praying alone, Kabbalat Shabbat, Lecha Dodi and Psalm 92. Today, thank one person for something slow and steady they do. Day six hundred sixteen.

howItsDone: Psalm 92, followed by Psalm 93, closes Kabbalat Shabbat on Friday night and is said again in the Shabbat morning service as the psalm of the day; many congregations sing it.

fork.setup: you're reading Psalm 92. the wicked seem to be winning, springing up everywhere. what does the psalm compare them to?
fork.reveal: grass. the righteous are the palm and the cedar: slow, deep-rooted, lasting.

original.note: Hebrew: it is good to give thanks. the opening of Psalm 92:2.

trapdoor: what you thought: a cheerful thank-you psalm.
what it means: a Sabbath look at what lasts, the palm tree, not the grass.
what a scholar hears: Mishnah Tamid 7:4 calls it a song for a world entirely at rest; Genesis Rabbah puts it in Adam's mouth after Cain's repentance.
